alternatives.why_less_likely: orders' own processing times remained low (e.g., orders-S00170 shows ~165 ms); the observed delay came from queuing, not intrinsic slowness.
many calls still reached orders (evidenced by orders-S00b5f etc.) and refused_calls were zero; timeouts without callee records were a minority and likely due to overload, not network loss.

causal_chain.claim: orders lost serving capacity; requests queued behind too few workers
orders processing latency increased due to queuing and a single worker
gateway timed out waiting for orders and returned 504 upstream_timeout errors to users

root_cause.summary: orders lost serving capacity due to a worker limit drop to 1, causing requests to queue and latency to spike, which led gateway calls to timeout.

verification.reason: disabling the matching condition(s) makes the incident disappear

alternatives.why_less_likely: The gateway deploy started at +53.799s, after latency had already begun rising (gateway-M000a at +53.304s shows high p50), so the deploy cannot be the initial cause.

causal_chain.claim: At +49.415s, an ops event throttled CPU for the orders service.
After the throttling, orders service metrics show workers_limit dropped from 16 to 1 starting at +51.635s.
With only one worker, orders request latency increased and queue length grew, as seen in orders-M000b (+56.635s) where p50=2288ms, p99=3172ms, queue_max=60.
The gateway began logging upstream timeout errors when calling orders, starting around +54.429s (e.g., gateway-L00070).
These timeouts resulted in 504 errors returned to users, visible in gateway metrics where err5xx rose to 79 at +58.304s (gateway-M000b).

root_cause.summary: CPU throttling reduced the orders service worker pool to 1, causing queue buildup and slow responses that led to gateway timeouts and user‑visible errors.
